items.title: 4.5 Adjoint and Inverse of a Square Matrix

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: For numbers, the inverse of 5 is \(\frac{1}{5}\) because \(5 \times \frac{1}{5} = 1\). For matrices the role of 1 is played by the identity matrix \(I\), and the inverse \(A^{-1}\) is the matrix with \(AA^{-1} = I\). To build \(A^{-1}\) we use the cofactors of 4.4.1 again.
then the matrix of co-factors of \(A\) =
\[\operatorname{adj} A = \begin{bmatrix} A_{11} & A_{21} & A_{31} \\ A_{12} & A_{22} & A_{32} \\ A_{13} & A_{23} & A_{33} \end{bmatrix}\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Compare the two matrices: \(\operatorname{adj} A\) (the adjoint of \(A\)) is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors. The cofactors of row 1 of \(A\) stand in column 1 of \(\operatorname{adj} A\), those of row 2 in column 2, and those of row 3 in column 3.
Inverse of a Square Matrix of Order n ≥ 3

Let \(A\) be a non singular (\(|A| \ne 0\)) square matrix of order \(n\). If there exists a matrix \(B\) such that \(AB = BA = I_{n}\), then \(B\) is called the multiplicative inverse of \(A\) and is denoted by \(A^{-1}\). It is obvious that the order of \(A^{-1}\) is \(n \times n\).
Thus, \(AA^{-1} = I_{n}\) and \(A^{-1}A = I_{n}\).
If \(A\) is non singular matrix then

blocks.text_alt: A inverse equals one over the determinant of A, times adjoint of A

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why does the formula work? Multiply \(A\) by \(\operatorname{adj} A\). Each diagonal entry is (a row of \(A\)) times (its own cofactors), which is the expansion of \(|A|\). Each off-diagonal entry is a row times the cofactors of a different row, which is the expansion of a determinant with two identical rows, so it is 0 (property iii). Hence
\[A(\operatorname{adj} A) = |A|\,I\]
and dividing by \(|A|\) gives \(A\left(\frac{1}{|A|}\operatorname{adj} A\right) = I\).
This is also why \(|A| \ne 0\) is needed: we cannot divide by zero. A matrix with \(|A| = 0\) is called singular and has no inverse.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Steps to find \(A^{-1}\) (order 3):
1. Find \(|A|\). If it is 0, stop: there is no inverse.
2. Find all nine cofactors \(A_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}\).
3. Write the matrix of cofactors and take its transpose: this is \(\operatorname{adj} A\).
4. Divide every entry of \(\operatorname{adj} A\) by \(|A|\).
5. Check: \(AA^{-1} = I\).
Example 7 below follows these steps. In the book's scan the labels and powers of the cofactors \(A_{23}\) and \(A_{32}\) are blurred; we have derived them (see the correction after the example).

blocks.title: Example 7
steps:
Given: \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
To find: \(A^{-1}\).
Method: \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|}\operatorname{adj} A\). So we need (1) all nine cofactors, (2) \(\operatorname{adj} A\), the transpose of the matrix of cofactors, (3) \(|A|\), which must not be 0.

Step 1: Cofactors of row 1
\[A_{11} = (-1)^{1+1}\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\]
\[= 1(2 + 1) = 3\]
\[A_{12} = (-1)^{1+2}\begin{vmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\]
\[= (-1)(-1) = 1\]
\[A_{13} = (-1)^{1+3}\begin{vmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 \end{vmatrix}\]
\[= 1(0 - 2) = -2\]
Why: \(A_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}\), and each minor is found by deleting row \(i\) and column \(j\) of \(A\).

Step 2: Cofactors of row 2
\[A_{21} = (-1)^{2+1}\begin{vmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\]
\[= (-1)(0 + 2) = -2\]
\[A_{22} = (-1)^{2+2}\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\]
\[= 1(1 - 2) = -1\]
\[A_{23} = (-1)^{2+3}\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 \end{vmatrix}\]
\[= (-1)(-1 - 0) = 1\]
Why: same rule. For \(A_{23}\) delete row 2 and column 3: the entries \(1, 0, 1, -1\) are left, and \(2 + 3 = 5\) is odd, so the sign changes.

Step 3: Cofactors of row 3
\[A_{31} = (-1)^{3+1}\begin{vmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\]
\[= 1(0 - 4) = -4\]
\[A_{32} = (-1)^{3+2}\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\]
\[= (-1)(1 - 0) = -1\]
\[A_{33} = (-1)^{3+3}\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{vmatrix}\]
\[= 1(2 - 0) = 2\]
Why: same rule. For \(A_{32}\) delete row 3 and column 2: the entries \(1, 2, 0, 1\) are left, and \(3 + 2 = 5\) is odd.

Step 4: The matrix of cofactors and its transpose
\[[A_{ij}]_{3 \times 3} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 & -2 \\ -2 & -1 & 1 \\ -4 & -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\]
\[\operatorname{adj} A = [A'_{ij}]_{3 \times 3}\]
\[= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 & -4 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\]
Why: \(\operatorname{adj} A\) is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors (\(A'_{ij} = A_{ji}\)): the first row \(3, 1, -2\) becomes the first column, and so on.

Step 5: The determinant
\[|A| = a_{11}A_{11} + a_{12}A_{12} + a_{13}A_{13}\]
\[= 1(3) + 0(1) + 2(-2)\]
\[= 3 + 0 - 4 = -1\]
Why: expand along row 1, using the cofactors already found. \(|A| = -1 \ne 0\), so \(A\) is non-singular and \(A^{-1}\) exists.

Step 6: The inverse
\[A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|}\operatorname{adj} A\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{-1}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 & -4 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\]
\[= \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 2 & 4 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\]
Why: dividing by \(-1\) changes the sign of every entry of \(\operatorname{adj} A\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
In Example 7 the labels of two cofactors print blurred: one reads like \(A_{3} = (-1)^{2+}\dots\) and the other like \(A_{2} = (-1)^{3\,2}\dots\). From their position and their minors they are
\(A_{23} = (-1)^{2+3}\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 \end{vmatrix} = (-1)(-1 - 0) = 1\) and
\(A_{32} = (-1)^{3+2}\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = (-1)(1 - 0) = -1\).
The values 1 and \(-1\) printed in the book are correct, and so is the final \(A^{-1}\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Matrix of cofactors: replace each element by its cofactor.
2. \(\operatorname{adj} A\) = transpose of the matrix of cofactors.
3. \(A^{-1}\) exists only if \(|A| \ne 0\) (non-singular matrix).
4. \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{|A|}\operatorname{adj} A\), and \(AA^{-1} = A^{-1}A = I\).
5. \(A(\operatorname{adj} A) = |A|\,I\); in Example 7 this is \(-I\).
6. Always check by multiplying \(A\) and \(A^{-1}\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Forgetting to transpose: the matrix of cofactors itself is NOT \(\operatorname{adj} A\).
2. Forgetting the signs \((-1)^{i+j}\), i.e. using minors instead of cofactors.
3. Dividing by \(|A|\) when \(|A| = 0\): a singular matrix has no inverse.
4. Dividing only some entries by \(|A|\): every entry of \(\operatorname{adj} A\) is divided.
5. Writing \(A^{-1} = \frac{1}{A}\): division by a matrix is not defined.
